food.text: Arabia's economy varied sharply by region. In South Arabia, farming depended on dams, floodwater diversion, terraces and wells, while in northern and western Arabia oasis towns, pastoral groups, caravan routes and seasonal markets linked local economies with wider exchange networks.

Farming in ancient Arabia varied sharply from place to place. In South Arabia and parts of eastern Arabia, agriculture depended on dams, floodwater diversion, terraces, wells and oasis systems. Managing scarce water was central to putting food on the table.

Long-distance trade mattered in pre-Islamic Arabia, but it was only one part of economic life. Local economies also depended on animal husbandry, oasis agriculture and the management of scarce water resources.

Al-Ula was a market city on the historic incense trade route. The route linked India and the Persian Gulf to the Levant and Europe, and carried spices, silk and other luxury items through Aksum, Arabia, Egypt and India.

One account says the food structure of Persian-Arabian civilization began with cooking techniques innovated in ancient Persia. Persians then carried these techniques forward during the Sassanid Dynasty. Much of the later culinary heritage of Eastern Arabia traces back to this Persian root.

Permanent oasis settlement in central Arabia developed later than in eastern and northern Arabia. It rested especially on date palms, cereals, camels, sheep and goats. Sites such as Zubayda, al-Uyun and Qaryat al-Faw grew gradually along the Jabal Tuwayq.

The Book of Ezekiel lists goods that Arabian peoples traded. Arabia and the princes of Kedar did business in lambs, rams and goats, while the merchants of Sheba and Raamah exchanged the finest of all kinds of spices, along with precious stones and gold.

The walled oasis city of al-Ula was founded in a desert valley with fertile soil and plenty of water. It stood near a palm grove that allowed its settlement, on the site of the Biblical city of Dedan.

Eastern Arabians once relied heavily on dates, wheat, barley, rice and meat, with little variety and a strong emphasis on yogurt products such as leben. Contact with ancient civilizations such as the Romans and Persians brought them into close contact with the dishes of other cultures. It also introduced several new ingredients into their diet.

The Chinese explorer Faxian, who passed through Sri Lanka in 414 CE, reported that Sabaean merchants and Arabs from Oman and Hadhramaut lived in ornate homes in settlements on the island. They traded in timber.

At al-Yamama in the al-Kharj oasis, archaeobotanical and archaeozoological evidence shows permanent occupation from the second half of the first millennium BCE. Its farming relied on date palms and cereals, especially barley and wheat, alongside sheep, goats and camels.

Rock engravings around al-Ula from the Iron Age to the pre-Islamic period put domesticated camels at over 50% of identifiable animals. They are shown in herds and with riders, a sign of how central the animals were to life there.

Eastern Arabian cuisine is said to trace part of its food structure to cooking techniques innovated in ancient Persia. Persians carried these techniques forward during the Sassanid Dynasty, shaping a shared Persian-Arabian culinary tradition.

Rock art near al-Ula from the pre-Islamic era shows ibex hunting with dogs. It also has ostrich motifs, including hunting scenes, possible herding and eggs, hinting at wild animals in the local world of food and hunting.

art.text: Old Arabian art first flourished at the beginning of the 1st millennium BC, in the South Arabian classical culture centred on the kingdoms of the Sabaeans and Minaeans in modern Yemen. The 5th century BC marked the golden age of Saba, whose main centres were Ma'rib and Sirwah.

Around Najran in southwest Arabia, as many as 6,400 human and animal illustrations have been recorded on rock. They include more than 1,800 camels and 1,300 human depictions. Bir Hima is among the region's richest rock art sites, and only the Jubba region has more petroglyphs.
art.source_title: Bir Hima Rock Petroglyphs and Inscriptions

art.text: The great Temple of Awwam in Ma'rib dates from the 9th to 5th centuries BC. It was an oval ashlar structure over 100 metres long, joined to a rectangular entrance hall surrounded by a peristyle of 32 monolithic pillars, each 5 metres high. Only a few traces remain today.

The Romans called South Arabia 'Arabia Felix', meaning Fortunate Arabia, because of its wealth. Its art flourished from the start of the 1st millennium BC, centred on the kingdoms of the Sabaeans and Minaeans. The 5th century BC was the golden age of Saba, whose main centres were Ma'rib and Sirwah.

Columns were a key structural element in South Arabia. Until the 5th century BC they were undecorated monoliths with rectangular or square cross-sections, as in the Awwam temple entrance hall. Afterwards the corners were reduced until the columns became round, and from the 2nd century BC Hellenistic architecture strongly influenced their forms.

The oldest South Arabian sanctuaries were simple stone monoliths, sometimes ringed by stone circles or mortarless masonry walls. In a second phase, actual temples appeared: simple rectangular stone structures without roofs. Their interiors differed widely from one another at first.

The Nabataean kingdom, established in northern Arabia in the late 4th century BC, acted as an intermediary between Arabian cultures and those of the Mediterranean. It helped carry artistic influences between the two worlds.

South Arabian temples began as simple stone monoliths, sometimes ringed by stone circles. Later came roofless rectangular stone temples. The great Temple of Awwam in Ma'rib dates from the 9th to 5th centuries BC and had an entrance hall surrounded by 32 monolithic pillars, each 5 metres high.

Saba had its own temple type with a rectangular plan and a propylon, divided into an inner courtyard with pillars on three sides and a tripartite cella. Examples include the moon god Wadd's temple, built around 700 BC, Qarnawu in the 5th century BC, and Al-Huqqa in the 1st century BC.

The Barran Temple, dedicated to Almaqah and shortly west of the Awwam Temple, is the best studied South Arabian temple. Its predecessors go back to the 10th century BCE, and inscriptions document its construction. It was destroyed shortly before the Christian era, possibly linked to the Roman siege led by Aelius Gallus in 25/24 BCE.

When Bir Hima's petroglyphs were first found in the 1950s, they showed weapons of war and hunting: daggers and swords, bows with arrows tipped with transverse arrowheads, sickle swords and throw-sticks. The images were dated 300 to 200 BC and interpreted as symbolic of spiritual animism. One expedition member recorded 250 images at a site west of the ancient wells.
art.source_title: Bir Hima Rock Petroglyphs and Inscriptions

art.text: The temple of the moon god Wadd was built around 700 BC between Ma'rib and Sirwah at Wadd ḏū-Masmaʿ. It belongs to a temple type found only in Saba, with an inner courtyard with pillars on three sides and a tripartite cella.

Cotton textiles were found in tombs at Hegra, where cotton remains date to the early first millennium CE. At Qal'at al-Bahrain, cotton seeds, textile fragments and textile tools date from the Achaemenid period. Together they place the Arabian Peninsula among the cotton-producing areas of the ancient Middle East.

war.text: Shortly after Rome annexed Egypt in 30 BCE, the Roman emperor Augustus ordered the Prefect of Egypt, Aelius Gallus, to lead an expedition into Arabia. Gallus invaded the south and captured major cities including Najran and Baraqish. During his siege of Marib, however, he had to turn back because of a growing number of problems besetting the expedition, especially water shortage.

In 106 AD the Romans annexed the Nabataean Kingdom under Trajan. Two legions closed in from different directions: the Third Cyrenaica from Egypt advanced on Bostra, and the Sixth Ferrata from Syria advanced on Petra. There may have been little resistance, since the former royal troops of Nabataea were joined into the Roman forces.

The Himyarite kingdom of South Arabia grew by conquest. It took neighbouring Saba' in about 25 BCE, Qataban in about 200 CE, and Hadramawt around 300 CE. By the late third century it had established supremacy over most of South Arabia.

Rabbel II ruled the Nabataean Kingdom from 70 AD until his death in early 105. After he died, a succession crisis followed. Trajan refused to recognize any of the claimants and sent his army to annex the kingdom instead.

Hadramawt repelled a Himyarite invasion toward the end of the 1st century BCE and annexed Qataban in the second half of the 2nd century CE, reaching its greatest size. It was continuously at war with Himyar and Saba' during this period. It was eventually conquered by the Himyarite king Shammar Yuhar'ish around 300 CE, unifying all of the south Arabic kingdoms.

Between 700 and 680 BC, the Kingdom of Awsan dominated Aden and its surroundings and challenged Sabaean supremacy in South Arabia. The Sabaean Mukarrib Karib'il Watar I conquered Awsan, and the city seems to have been destroyed in the 7th century BCE, according to a Sabaean text that reports the victory in terms that show how much it meant to the Sabaeans. He expanded Sabaean rule over much of South Arabia, but lack of water kept the Sabaeans from unifying the entire peninsula, so they set up colonies to control trade routes.
The Sabaean king Sha'irum Awtar was able to take the Hadramawt capital, Shabwah, in 225. During this same period the Kingdom of Aksum began to interfere in South Arabian affairs.

King GDRT of Aksum sent troops under his son, BYGT, into South Arabia. Some went from the western coast to occupy Thifar, the Himyarite capital. Others went from the southern coast against Hadramawt, acting as Sabaean allies.

literature.text: Almost no literary manuscripts from pre-Islamic Arabia have survived, so historians study its writing through inscriptions. These are attested from at least the early 1st millennium BC until the early Islamic period.

Ancient South Arabian scripts were consonantal alphabets used from approximately the 9th century BC to the 6th century AD. They were written from right to left and consisted of 29 distinct letters. They wrote languages such as Sabaic, Minaic, Qatabanic and Hadramautic.
No substantial body of Old South Arabian literary texts, such as myths or epics, has survived. If such literature was ever written down, it is not represented in the known inscriptions.

The Ancient South Arabian script had two forms. The monumental form, called musnad, was carved on stone, rock and metal. A cursive form, often called zabur, was used on wooden sticks and palm-leaf stalks for letters, legal texts and other everyday documents.

Ancient North Arabian scripts were used in northern and central Arabia between roughly the 8th century BC and the 4th century AD. Unlike the South Arabian scripts, they were more often used for graffiti than for formal monumental inscriptions. Major forms include Safaitic, Hismaic and Dadanitic.

The Nabataean script developed from Imperial Aramaic and was used by the Nabataean Kingdom. Between the third century and the mid-fifth century it evolved into Nabataeo-Arabic, which mixes Aramaic features with notable features of the later fully developed Arabic script.

Ancient South Arabian scripts were consonantal alphabets of 29 letters, used from about the 9th century BC to the 6th century AD. They were written right to left, though boustrophedon is occasionally attested early on. They served for monumental inscriptions and religious dedications across the kingdoms of South Arabia.

The latest securely dated Sabaic inscription was written in 559 CE. Sabaic had a long history, with its earliest phase often dated to the eighth century BCE and its best-documented period, Middle Sabaic, running from about the third century BCE to the mid-fourth century CE.

The Namara inscription of 328 CE is one of two important Old Arabic inscriptions written in the Nabataean script, alongside the ʿEn ʿAvdat inscription. Such brief texts illuminate the gradual emergence of Arabic as a written language and the transition from Nabataean to Arabic script.
The Hymn of Qāniya is a twenty-seven line poem known from a first century rock, addressed to the god Shams. It is the earliest evidence for pre-Islamic poetry, which comes from ancient inscriptions.

The earliest known example of cursive Nabataean script was found at Horvat Raqiq, near Beersheba. Unlike most Nabataean inscriptions, it was not engraved but written in ink applied directly to a large rock.

science.text: The Sabaeans built the Marib Dam to capture the region's monsoon rains and irrigate farmland around their capital, Marib. The most reliable dating places the dam's construction at about the 8th century BC.

The Nabataeans of Petra survived the surrounding desert through efficient rainwater collection and desert farming. This water technology helped support a population that peaked at an estimated 20,000 people in the 1st century AD.

Frankincense resin was harvested from Boswellia trees in southern Arabia, as the Greek historian Herodotus recorded in his History. The resin was then hand-sorted for quality, with grades varying by the time of harvest.

Sabir culture, found along the Red Sea coastal plain of Yemen and southern Saudi Arabia, has major phases dated by excavation and radiocarbon to 1900 to 800 cal BC. Its sedentary settlements show hut architecture, irrigation and layered habitation deposits. Archaeologists define its phases using pottery typologies.

Sabaean kings repeatedly repaired the Marib Dam to keep it working. King Yatha' Amar Watar I, who reigned from 760 to 740 BC, left the dam's earliest known inscription, marking its construction or repair.

Around 115 BC the Himyarites took control of the Marib Dam and rebuilt it into a structure 14 metres high, with five spillway channels, two masonry-reinforced sluices and a 1,000-metre canal. The work was not finished until 325 AD, and it irrigated about 100 square kilometres of farmland.

Along Yemen's Red Sea coast, the Sabir culture, dated to between 1900 and 800 BC, built sedentary settlements with hut architecture and irrigation. Its people also raised standing stones known as menhirs on the Tihamah plain, likely for ritual or territorial marking.

politics.text: In 106 CE the Roman emperor Trajan annexed the Nabataean Kingdom and turned it into the province of Arabia Petraea. The last Nabataean king, Rabbel II, had died in early 105, and a succession crisis followed. Trajan refused to recognize any of the claimants.

The kingdom of Himyar in the Yemeni highlands rose from being part of Qataban until around 110 BCE to supremacy over most of South Arabia by the late third century CE. It conquered Saba' around 25 BCE for the first time, Qataban around 200 CE, and Hadramawt around 300 CE.

Augustus, the first Roman emperor, ordered Aelius Gallus, the Prefect of Egypt, to lead an expedition into Arabia. Gallus invaded the south and captured major cities including Najran and Baraqish. During his siege of Marib, a growing number of problems besetting the expedition, above all water shortage, ultimately forced him to turn back.

The Roman conquest of Nabataea was launched from two directions. The Third Cyrenaica legion advanced from Egypt onto Bostra, while the Sixth Ferrata legion moved from Syria toward Petra. There may have been little resistance, since the former royal troops of Nabataea were joined into the Roman forces.

Hadramawt was the last South Arabian kingdom to fall to Himyar. It had repelled Himyarite attacks in the 1st century BCE and annexed Qataban in the 2nd century CE, reaching its greatest size. Then the Himyarite king Shammar Yahri'sh invaded in the 3rd century CE.

Around 200 to 230, King Gedara of Aksum became the first Aksumite king involved in South Arabian affairs. His reign brought control of much of western Yemen, including the Tihama and Najran. A joint Himyarite-Sabean alliance eventually pushed the Aksumites out, and conflict between Aksum and Himyar continued through the 3rd century.

The Kingdom of Qedar was the most organized of the northern Arabian tribes. At its height in the 6th century BCE it spanned a large area between the Persian Gulf and the Sinai. Its monarchs first appear in Assyrian inscriptions, and some early rulers were Assyrian vassals who later revolted against Assyria.

Local communities quickly adopted a new dating system, the Bostran era, whose first year began in 106 AD, when the province was created. Some people kept writing in Nabataean, yet a public Nabataean ethnic identity declined in documents right after the conquest.

In northwestern Arabia, the kingdom of Lihyan, centered at Dedan (modern al-'Ula), flourished between the 6th and 2nd centuries BCE. It left numerous inscriptions and monumental tombs. The Nabataeans later expanded into the northwestern Hejaz, controlling caravan routes and the oasis of Hegra until the Roman annexation in 106 CE.

Arabia Petraea was a key province along the Limes Arabicus, which marked the Roman Empire's border across the Arabian Desert. It was the only Near Eastern province that Rome did not gain and then lose during Trajan's reign, unlike Armenia, Assyria and Mesopotamia.

The kingdom of Himyar officially adopted Judaism in the fourth century CE. This tied it to Jewish communities in northwestern Arabian oases such as Yathrib, later called Medina, as well as Khaybar and Tayma.

philosophy.text: Until about the fourth century CE, almost all inhabitants of Arabia practiced polytheistic religions. After that, belief in a single God began to spread. Recent scholarship suggests that henotheism or monotheism was dominant from the fourth century onwards, overturning the older view.

Inscriptions across the Arabian Peninsula show gods and idols fading from the record after the fourth century. South Arabian inscriptions are almost exclusively monotheistic by the fourth century. In North Arabia, inscriptions are entirely monotheistic by the sixth century, before the advent of Islam.

Judaism was the first monotheistic religion practiced in pre-Islamic Arabia, predating the Common Era. Its main centers were in the northwest and south of the peninsula. Arabian Jews spoke Greek, Aramaic, Arabic and Sabaic.

In the second half of the fourth century, the ruling elite of Himyar abandoned the traditional pantheon and adopted Judaism. Yet explicitly Jewish inscriptions by the elite are not common, and most present a neutral monotheism. Possible reasons include a superficial use of Judaism, or a general cult of one God as a way to keep the diverse kingdom united.

In South Arabia, all gods quickly cease to be mentioned in the second half of the fourth century except for Rahmanan. Elsewhere, especially in northern and western Arabia, inscriptions begin to invoke only Allah by the fifth and sixth centuries.

Not all Arabian monotheists were Christians or Jews. Gentile monotheists are called hanif in Islamic sources. Their existence shows that the turn to one God was broader than the two major Abrahamic religions.

Before the fourth century, religion in Sabaean South Arabia centered on Almaqah, the principal god of the Sabaeans, who served as a dynastic and national deity. His major cult centers were at Marib and Sirwah, including the Temple of Awwam. The astral god 'Athtar, linked to rain, fertility and warfare, was worshipped across several South Arabian polities.

Local Jewish leadership is attested in northwestern Arabia. One inscription from 203 AD states that a Jew named Isaiah became head of the Tayma oasis. Inscriptions from the mid-4th century refer to Jewish headmen of both Hegra and Dedan.

Judaism briefly gained political ascendancy in South Arabia, starting in the late fourth century when Malkikarib Yuhamin converted to the religion. Christianity also grew there, and heavy resistance to it prompted a massacre of the Christian community of Najran in the early sixth century under Dhu Nuwas. The massacre prompted an invasion of Himyar by the Christian Aksumite Kingdom, which ended Jewish ascendancy and ushered in Christian rule during the 520s.

The origins of Arabian Judaism are not well understood. Some have speculated that these communities arose from people fleeing persecution during Babylonian, Roman and other periods, though no evidence supports any theory. No pre-Islamic translations of Jewish scriptures into Arabian languages have been found, suggesting their religious culture was largely oral.

Northwestern Arabian inscriptions trace the shift from Nabataean Aramaic to Arabic writing, known in its late antique form as Paleo-Arabic. The same material shows changes in religious vocabulary, including a reduced number of named divine figures in the later inscriptions.

Excavations at Wadi Musa in southern Jordan uncovered a bronze oil burner bearing a dedication by a priest and his son to the god Obodas. It dates to the reign of the Nabataean king Rabbel II Soter, who ruled from 70 to 106 AD.

culture.text: Until around the fourth century CE, nearly all of the inhabitants of Arabia practiced polytheism. After that, Christianity spread significantly in the north between the fourth and sixth centuries. Inscriptions show polytheistic gods and idols ceasing to be mentioned.

Safaitic graffiti number in the tens of thousands, found in the basalt deserts of southern Syria, northeastern Jordan and northern Saudi Arabia. They were typically incised by pastoral nomads. The inscriptions record personal names, genealogies, prayers, curses and accounts of daily life.

The Kaaba in Mecca was a center of Arab polytheism, which venerated gods and goddesses such as Hubal, al-Lāt, al-‘Uzzā, and Manāt. The Kaaba is said to have contained up to 360 idols. Worshippers honored their deities through pilgrimages, divination, and ritual sacrifice. Camels, sheep and cattle were killed as offerings, and the victim's blood was 'poured out' on the altar stone to form a bond between the human and the deity. Human sacrifice was sometimes carried out in Arabia, the victims generally being prisoners of war.

The Nabataean city of Hegra holds more than 110 well-preserved tombs carved into sandstone outcrops. The dry climate, the lack of resettlement after abandonment, and local beliefs about the place all helped preserve it. The site has a reputation as a cursed place because, according to the Quran, the Thamudis who lived there were punished by God for their idolatry. They had killed a sacred camel, and an earthquake and lightning blasts struck them dead.

Petra was known to its own people as Raqmu and is nicknamed the "Rose City" for the colour of its sandstone. The Nabataeans survived in the desert thanks to efficient rainwater collecting and desert farming. At its peak in the 1st century AD, Petra had an estimated 20,000 inhabitants.

Judaism is attested in Arabia since the 1st century BC and was the first form of monotheism documented there. It briefly gained political ascendancy in South Arabia from the late fourth century, when Malkikarib Yuhamin converted. Heavy resistance to a growing Christianity then prompted Dhu Nuwas to massacre the Christian community of Najran in the early sixth century, and the massacre prompted the Aksumite invasion of Himyar that brought Christian rule.

At Qaryat al-Faw, archaeologists found a temple of the sun god Shams containing a mrzḥ, a ritual banqueting institution. By the Roman period it had absorbed Hellenistic forms such as the symposium. It is the easternmost mrzḥ known from inscriptions, showing that Hellenized cult practices reached deep into central Arabia.

Kahl was the chief god of Qaryat al-Faw from the 2nd century BC, and the city was most often called "the City of Kahl." He appears on coins until the 1st century AD. A consistent image of a standing figure holding a weapon, perhaps a club, over his shoulder has been speculatively linked to him. This image resembles the smiting gods of West Asia and the Eastern Mediterranean.

Jewish communities existed across pre-Islamic Arabia, including both settled and nomadic groups. Arabian Jews spoke Arabic as well as Hebrew and Aramaic and kept contact with Jewish religious centres in Babylonia and Palestine. Tomb inscriptions show that Jews also lived at Mada'in Saleh and Al-'Ula.

Frescoes from the Temple of Shams at Qaryat al-Faw show human figures, camel drivers, and mythological motifs framed in cartouches with vines and grape clusters. One fragment carries the inscription 'zky, meaning "pious, blessed". Its artist may have trained in the painting workshops of Roman Egypt.

Christianity reached Petra during the 4th century AD, and the city converted gradually. At least one tomb, now called the Urn Tomb, was used as a church. A red-paint inscription records its consecration in 447 in the time of the "most holy bishop Jason."

A third-century AD Sabaic poem (Zaid Inan 11) shows the god Kahl leading an army of Sabaeans into Al-Yamama, then called al-Jaww. According to the poem, he pierces the region and conquers it in a triumphant victory, as part of his "rising in the East", meaning the overcoming of the night. In it Kahl absorbs the properties and functions of several earlier deities, and some historians see this as part of a trend in South Arabian religion toward pre-Islamic monotheism, with Kahl possibly becoming Rahmanan.

A first-century stonemason named Wahb'allahi worked in Hegra. An inscription names him as the responsible stonemason on the oldest datable tomb there, from the ninth year of the Nabataean king Aretas IV (1 BC/AD 1). He was the brother of the stonemason 'Abdharetat.

A bronze oil burner found in Wadi Musa carries a dedication to Obodas by a priest and his son. It dates to the reign of the Nabataean king Rabbel II Soter, who ruled between 70 and 106 AD. It is one of dozens of bronze fragments with Nabataean inscriptions found there.
